## Research question

How economically distant was the United States from other economies in **2019**, as measured by GDP per capita, GDP-deflator inflation, imports and exports? This is an updated R/Quarto analysis of an earlier class project coauthored with Xianghan Zhu. The analysis measures dissimilarity, not overall market attractiveness.

## Q1. Data and preparation

```{r}
#| label: load-analysis
source('R_analysis.R')
```

The source is the World Bank's World Development Indicators export. We use **GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$; NY.GDP.PCAP.KD)**, not aggregate GDP, together with GDP-deflator inflation and imports/exports as percentages of GDP. See [Data & methodology](methods.qmd) for indicator definitions and decisions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-audit
#| tbl-cap: "2019 sample audit"
audit <- data.frame(
  stage = c('Country/economy codes in source', 'Recognized countries/economies',
            'Complete observations', 'Incomplete observations removed',
            'Excluded aggregate/unrecognized codes'),
  count = c(nrow(wide), nrow(country_data), nrow(complete_data),
            nrow(excluded_incomplete), nrow(excluded_aggregates))
)
knitr::kable(audit)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-missing
#| tbl-cap: "Available and missing values by indicator (individual economies before complete-case filtering)"
knitr::kable(missingness)
```

## Q2. Descriptive statistics

The following statistics are calculated on **one common complete-case sample**, using original units rather than standardized values. GDP per capita is in constant 2015 US dollars; all other indicators are in percentage units.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-descriptive
#| tbl-cap: "Summary of 2019 economic indicators"
knitr::kable(summary_stats, digits = 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-distributions
#| fig-cap: "2019 distributions of four economic indicators (original units; scales differ)"
#| fig-height: 8
complete_data %>%
  select(all_of(indicators)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = 'indicator', values_to = 'value') %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = '#447C91', color = 'white') +
  facet_wrap(~indicator, scales = 'free', ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = '2019 indicator value', y = 'Number of economies')
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-correlations
#| tbl-cap: "Pearson correlations among economic indicators, complete 2019 sample"
knitr::kable(round(correlation, 3))
```

*Interpretation to complete after rendering:* Discuss the central tendency, spread, outliers and strongest correlations using actual values from the tables. A correlation does not establish causation.

## Q3. Mahalanobis distance

For country $i$, the US reference vector $x_{US}$ and the sample covariance matrix $S$:

$$D(i,US)=\sqrt{(x_i-x_{US})^{\mathsf{T}}S^{-1}(x_i-x_{US})}.$$

Unlike unscaled Euclidean distance, Mahalanobis distance accounts for different variances and correlations among the four indicators. The covariance matrix is computed from the retained 2019 country sample. We take the square root of R's squared Mahalanobis distance. **Distance is descriptive and does not directly measure business risk or cultural and legal differences.**

```{r}
#| label: tbl-distance-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Mahalanobis distances from the United States; USA excluded"
knitr::kable(distance_summary, digits = 3)
```

## Q4. Closest and farthest economies

```{r}
#| label: tbl-closest
#| tbl-cap: "Ten closest economies to the United States in 2019"
knitr::kable(closest, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-farthest
#| tbl-cap: "Ten farthest economies from the United States in 2019"
knitr::kable(farthest, digits = 3)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ranked
#| fig-cap: "Three closest and three farthest economies to the USA"
plot_data <- bind_rows(
  head(closest, 3) %>% mutate(group = 'Closest'),
  head(farthest, 3) %>% mutate(group = 'Farthest')
)
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = reorder(country, distance_us), y = distance_us)) +
  geom_col(fill = '#447C91') + coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~group, scales = 'free_y', ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = 'Mahalanobis distance from the USA')
```

*Interpretation to complete after rendering:* Name the three closest and three farthest countries and explain their differences in terms of **the measured variables**. Check whether unusual observations affect rankings.

## Q5. International expansion recommendation

*Evidence-based recommendation to complete:* Select a clearly defined industry and potential host economy; reference the **actual distance rank** and add independent evidence on market size, growth, regulation and market entry costs. A low distance score alone is not proof of investment attractiveness. Avoid recommending a country by incorrectly claiming it is the closest when the ranking disagrees.

## Limitations and references

Results cover only 2019, omit economies with missing observations, and depend on the choice of indicators and covariance sample. GDP per capita describes average output per person, not total market size. Import/export shares describe trade openness, not bilateral US trade ties. This specification is an operationalization for the assignment, not necessarily an exact reproduction of the authors' published index.

Berry, H., Guillén, M. F., & Zhou, N. (2010). An institutional approach to cross-national distance. *Journal of International Business Studies, 41*(9), 1460–1480. https://doi.org/10.1057/jibs.2010.28

World Bank. *World Development Indicators*. https://databank.worldbank.org/source/world-development-indicators
